background.definition: Uterine leiomyomas or fibroids are benign smooth muscular outgrowths of the uterine wall.

list.listitem: At 12-year follow-up of 23,505 premenopausal Black women aged 23 to 50 years participating in the Black Women's Health Study, 7268 new fibroids (30.9%) were diagnosed.

In a longitudinal cohort study of 1,241 individuals aged 23-35 years who self-identified as Black and underwent up to five transvaginal ultrasonograms over 10 years of follow up, the overall incidence rate of uterine leiomyomas was 54 cases per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 49-60).
The incidence of sonographically-detected myomas in pregnancy is low (1.5%).
Twenty-five percent to 35% of women older than 35 years have fibroids, although many are asymptomatic; 70% of white women and 80% of black women have fibroids by age 50 years.
In a population-based study of 1364 women, just over half the women without a previous diagnosis of fibroids had fibroids present on ultrasound.

In a study of 100 consecutive women having hysterectomy, myomas were found in 77% (some only 2 mm in size). Premenopausal women had an average of 7.6 myomas, and postmenopausal women had an average of 4.2 myomas.

Estimated annual direct costs of uterine fibroids (due to surgery, hospital admissions, outpatient visits, and medications) were $4.1 to 9.4 billion in 2010 US dollars and annual estimated lost work-hour costs ranged from $1.55 to 17.2 billion.
Most common female pelvic tumor.
One-third to one-half of the approximately 600,000 hysterectomies performed annually in the United States are for symptomatic fibroids.

There is a modest association between fibroids and hypertension. In a cross-sectional Chinese study including 1617 patients with uterine fibroids on clinical examination and 6784 patients without fibroids the odds ratio [OR] was 1.35, 95% CI 1.02-1.79; a meta-analysis performed by the same authors confirmed the association with hypertension but with significant heterogeneity (pooled OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.17-1.75, I2 = 68%).

Submucous myomas decrease fertility and may impair implantation rates in women undergoing assisted reproduction (OR 0.6; 95% CI, 0.5-0.8). In a systematic review of observational studies of in vitro fertilization, there was a significant decrease in the live birth (RR 0.8; 95% CI, 0.7-0.9) and clinical pregnancy rates (RR 0.85; 95% CI, 0.8-0.9) in women with noncavity-distorting intramural fibroids compared with those without fibroids.
Cases of hemoperitoneum following posttraumatic avulsion of a pedunculate fibroid and pyomyoma have been reported.

Based on data from the US Nurses' Health Study II including 110,091 women aged 25-42 years in 1989, subsequent ultrasound or hysterectomy-confirmed uterine fibroids while not associated with all cause premature mortality was associated with a greater risk of cause-specific mortality from malignant neoplasm of gynecological organs (hazard ratio 2.3, 95% CI 1.6-3.4).
The cause is unknown.

Genetic factors appear to contribute to development of fibromas (see Pathophysiology). Mutations of mediator complex subunit 12 is reported in up to 85% of patients with fibroids and is more commonly found among Black (74.5%) as compared to White (65.8%) and Asian (53.2%) patients, based on a meta-analysis including 25 studies with 3151 tissue samples.

In a study exploring genome-wide association studies, there appears to be a reduced risk for uterine leiomyomata with older age at menarche and older age at first birth and increased risk with older age at natural menopause (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.06-1.09). This was also reported in a similar study in which a relationship was found for either decreased or increased risk of uterine leiomyoma and age at menarche (OR 0.84), age at menopause (OR 1.08), number of live births (OR 0.25) and total testosterone levels (OR 0.90).
Both estrogen and progesterone promote the development of fibromas.

Authors of a systematic review of data from registries or large population cohort studies identified age, premenopausal state, hypertension, family history, time since last birth, and food additive and soybean milk consumption as factors increasing uterine fibroid risk. Decreased risk was associated with use of oral contraceptives or the injectable contraceptive depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, smoking in women with low body mass index, and parity.

Fibroids are generally classified as pedunculated (attached to the uterus by a stalk), intramural (completely within the wall of the uterus), subserosal (on the outside surface of the uterus), or submucosal (rest against or project into the uterine cavity).
Fibroids are believed to contribute to heavy menstrual bleeding because of global enlargement of the uterus.

In a study of tissue samples from 114 uterine fibroids, erythropoietin mRNA expression was detected in 95%; expression was weakly correlated with leiomyoma size and associated with blood vessel maturity.

Studies on gene expression from tissue samples of fibroids and normal myometrium have found concordant changes in genes regulating retinoid synthesis, IGF metabolism, TGF-beta signaling, and extracellular matrix formation that may provide clues to the development of these tumors.

Many growth factors are overexpressed in myomas, which may promote cell proliferation. In one genome-wide linkage study, fatty acid synthase (FAS) was elevated 3-fold in fibroid-affected tissue compared to matched myometrial tissue; FAS transcripts are upregulated in various neoplasms and implicated in tumor cell survival.

list.listitem: Approximately half of women with fibroids have symptoms prompting medical attention. Symptoms include pelvic pain, urinary frequency, and AUB (primarily menorrhagia). The association between myomas and these symptoms, however, is questionable, as many patients are asymptomatic.
Fibroids do not appear to cause dyspareunia or sexual dysfunction.
On physical examination clinicians may detect an enlarged, irregular, firm, and nontender uterus indicative of subserosal or intramural fibroids.

Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is the initial diagnostic test of choice for women in whom a structural abnormality of the uterus is suspected based on history (eg, older age with menorrhagia) or physical examination (eg, enlarged uterus).

MRI can be used if sonography fails to identify the origin of a pelvic mass. American College of Radiology guidelines (ACR, 2022) note that when MRI is clinically useful, gadolinium-based IV contrast agent is preferred for identification of fibroid vascularity and other characteristics. In a small study, MRI was found to have higher sensitivity than ultrasound (80% vs 40%) and was suggested as the preferred diagnostic modality for clinical research.

T2-weighted MRI appears useful for differentiating uterine leiomyomas from leiomyosarcomas. Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies including 2253 patients with uterine leiomyomas and 179 with uterine sarcomas found high diagnostic accuracy in the differential diagnosis between uterine leiomyomas and sarcomas with MRI (diagnostic OR 175.1, 95% CI 46.5-659.1 and area under the curve of 0.98).

ACR guidelines (2022) recommend US or MRI without and with contrast as usually appropriate in patients with known fibroids for initial treatment planning or surveillance. They note that MRI is superior to transabdominal followed by TVUS for identifying and mapping fibroids, and alters management in up to 28% of patients.

Saline infusion sonography (SIS, also called hysterosonography and sonohysterography), a technique using infusion of 10 to 15 mL of saline through the cervix using a catheter while performing TVUS, can provide additional definition of intracavitary abnormalities. In studies of patients with AUB, sonohysterography had slightly higher diagnostic accuracy than TVUS. It is used by radiologists and gynecologists for evaluation of AUB and compares favorably with hysteroscopy, although diagnostic accuracy is slightly less for intrauterine fibroids.
Hysteroscopy, direct visualization of the uterine cavity through a small endoscope, is an excellent tool for diagnosing submucosal fibroids, performing better than TVUS or SIS.
The addition of three-dimensional gel instillation sonography did not change sensitivity or specificity in discriminating between fibroids and polyps or change planning for hysteroscopic procedures.

Negative findings on positron emission tomography (PET) with 2-deoxy-2-[(18)F]fluoro-D-glucose or PET with 3'-deoxy-3'-[(18)F]-fluorothymidine can be used to rule out malignancy for patients with suspected leiomyosarcoma.

Laboratory testing for CA-125 or the neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (≥2.12) may be useful in distinguishing between fibroids and uterine leiomyosarcoma. In one study, however, CA-125 was not predictive.
If symptomatic, patients may present with pelvic pain and/or AUB.
TVUS is the initial diagnostic test of choice.
SIS or hysteroscopy can be used for diagnosing submucosal fibroids in women with AUB.
The levonorgestrel intrauterine device (LNG-IUD) decreases uterine volume and blood loss in women with symptomatic fibroids. B
Mifepristone may be an alternate medical treatment. B

Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists can be used for up to 3 to 4 months to decrease fibroid and uterine size prior to surgery; their use can correct iron-deficiency anemia and reduce intraoperative blood loss. A

Gonadotropin releasing hormone antagonists combined with hormonal add-back therapy appear safe and effective for premenopausal women with symptomatic uterine fibroids. B Relugolix with add-back therapy is FDA-approved for use of up to 24 months in patients with fibroid-associated heavy menstrual bleeding.
Hysterectomy is optimal for women who no longer desire fertility and want definitive treatment. A
Myomectomy appears to have the lowest reintervention rates and highest fertility rates of the uterine-sparing procedures. B
UAE improves symptoms by 85% or more; it is associated with a higher rate of minor postsurgical complications and higher rates of unscheduled visits and readmission compared with hysterectomy. A
Ablative techniques also appear successful. B
Traditional management with combination oral contraceptives or progestins is not well supported in the literature but can be used to control bleeding.
NSAIDS taken during menses (eg, ibuprofen 400 mg 3 to 4 times daily) may decrease bleeding, but data are inconsistent.

The LNG-IUD was found to be effective in a study of women with symptomatic fibroids in decreasing uterine volume and blood loss. A systematic review of 11 RCTs confirmed less menstrual blood loss despite some occurrences of irregular bleeding; expulsion rates appear to be higher (11% vs 0-3% among women without fibroids). Cochrane authors, however, in their updated review of 4 studies with 221 patients with uterine fibroids found insufficient evidence to support use of either oral progestogens (two negative trials) or progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems (one positive trial) for uterine fibroids due to very low-quality data and no information on outcomes of interest.

In a Cochrane review of three small RCTs, mifepristone (5 mg or 10 mg daily) reduced heavy uterine bleeding and, in one trial, improved leiomyoma-related quality of life. There were no differences from placebo on fibroid or uterine volume. Pooled data suggest an increased risk of abnormal endometrial histology in the mifepristone group; in the RCT using 10 mg of mifepristone, 63% of women had endometrial hyperplasia.
In a fourth RCT, a 5 mg dose of mifepristone was as effective as 10 mg in reducing fibroid volume and symptoms; one case of endometrial hyperplasia was seen in a woman in the 10 mg group.

Investigators in a multicenter Chinese RCT found mifepristone 10 and 25 mg to be as effective as enantone, a gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, for reducing leiomyoma size and decreasing symptoms. Most women in all groups developed amenorrhea. Mifepristone 10 mg was associated with the fewer side effects compared to enantone and estradiol levels were maintained in the premenopausal range for both mifepristone doses.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies including 2066 patients found 3-month mifepristone treatment significantly better than 6-month treatment for smaller uterine volume with improved symptoms comparing mifepristone groups to controls. Adverse effects included hot flashes, endometrial thickness increases, and elevated hepatic transaminases compared to control groups; patients in the 10 mg/d mifepristone group had significantly increased endometrial thickness compared to those in the 5 mg/d mifepristone group.

GnRH antagonists have had a limited role in long-term management. Traditionally, they were used for 3 to 4 months to decrease fibroid and uterine size prior to surgery; their use can correct iron-deficiency anemia and reduce intraoperative blood loss.

GnRH antagonists result in rapid, reversible suppression of ovarian sex hormones. Relugolix is associated with dose-dependent reductions in bone mineral density (BMD). Once daily 40 mg relugolix in combination with estradiol 1 mg and norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg (add-back therapy) was shown to reduce bleeding in two 24-week phase 3 RCTs including 770 patients with fibroid-related heavy menstrual bleeding. Seventy-three percent and 71% of intervention patients in these trials had a reduced volume of menstrual blood loss <80 ml and a ≥50% reduction in volume from baseline compared to 19% and 15%, of those in the two placebo groups. Intervention patients also reported significantly improved pain, distress from bleeding and pelvic discomfort.

In the combined 24-week Liberty RCTs conducted with 509 premenopausal women with uterine fibroid-associated heavy menstrual bleeding, those on relugolix combination therapy showed a statistically significant reduction in symptom severity (-33.5 vs -12.1) and Health-Related Quality of Life scores from baseline to week 24 compared with placebo (+37.6 vs +13.1).

Women participating in this trial were invited to enroll in an extension of the above study, 477 agreed and 363 (76.1%) completed 52 weeks. Most women (87.7%) had improvement in heavy menstrual bleeding and over half (59%) had improvements in hemoglobin concentration of greater than 2 g/dL. Reduction of uterine leiomyoma-associated symptom burden was sustained. BMD was maintained and no new safety concerns were reported.

Similarly, in a 28-week extension of the 24-week RCT including 241 participants self-identified as Black or African American enrolled in the LIBERTY Long-Term Extension study, 64.3% of women achieved amenorrhea and 58 of 70 women (82.9%, 95% CI 72.0-90.8%) met the treatment responder criteria for reduction in heavy menstrual bleeding. The most frequently reported adverse events were hot flushes (12.9%), headache (5.7%), and hypertension (5.7%). Bone mineral density was preserved through 52 weeks.

In the 2-year relugolix combination therapy phase 3 LIBERTY randomized withdrawal study including 229 patients who met responder criteria, 69.8% of those who continued active treatment maintained menstrual blood loss volume <80 mL compared to 11.8% in the placebo group by week 104. Among the 89 women in the placebo group who relapsed and received open-label rescue treatment, 87 women responded to relugolix combination therapy. No new adverse effects were reported and bone mineral density was maintained.

Relugolix with add-back therapy, marketed as Myfembree, was FDA-approved in 2021 for use of up to 24 months in patients with fibroid-associated heavy menstrual bleeding with a warning of increased risk of thromboembolic events and potential risk of bone loss.

Elagolix, a GnRH antagonist used in the treatment of pain associated with endometriosis, was also successful in reducing heavy menstrual bleeding as monotherapy (300 mg dose) or with combination add-back therapy in two 6-month RCTs. Hot flushes were more common among patients receiving elagolix plus add-back therapy than with placebo in both trials. This drug, marketed as Oriahnn, was FDA-approved in 2020 for the management of heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine leiomyomas in premenopausal women for up to 24 months with warnings as noted for relugolix.

Lower dose elagolix (150 mg) was shown to be effective in reducing uterine bleeding in an RCT including 82 patients with heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids; 49% in the elagolix group (95% CI 35% - 64%) achieved the primary endpoint of menstrual blood loss volume <80 mL and at least a 50% reduction in menstrual blood loss volume from baseline to the final month vs. 23% in the placebo group (7% - 40%).

Another GnRH antagonist, linzagolix, was investigated in two 52-week phase 3 trials with 511/574 and 501/535 patients completing the trials. Patients were randomized to five masked treatments of placebo, monotherapy or various combined therapies. Linzagolix (100 mg or 200 mg) with or without add-back therapy significantly reduced heavy menstrual bleeding with response rates of 56.4% with lower dose and 77.7% with higher-dose monotherapy and 77.2% and 93.9% with combination therapy low and high doses, respectively. An application was submitted to the FDA seeking approval for treatment of uterine fibroids in Sept 2021 but withdrawn in 2022.

SERMs and antagonists have shown inconsistent results with some showing decreased uterine size. However, authors of a Cochrane review were unable to find high-quality data and concluded that there was no evidence that reducing fibroid size with SERMs improved clinical outcomes.
Selective progesterone receptor modulators may reduce leiomyoma cell proliferation and excessive uterine bleeding.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 882 participants with symptomatic uterine fibroids found ulipristal acetate (UPA) achieved amenorrhea (RR 24.5; 95% CI, 10.8-55.6), reduced blood loss, and improved quality of life compared to placebo. There was insufficient evidence from these RCTs to assess adverse events and insufficient evidence from the single trial comparing UPA with leuprolide acetate on outcomes.

In a non-inferiority RCT of 307 women with symptomatic fibroids, UPA (5 mg or 10 mg daily) was noninferior to once-monthly leuprolide acetate in controlling uterine bleeding and less likely to cause hot flashes (11% and 10% vs 40%, respectively).

In the most recently reported placebo-controlled RCT of 157 women, amenorrhea was achieved by 47.2% of those on 5 mg ulipristal and 58.3% on 10 mg ulipristal and both doses resulted in improved quality of life compared with placebo. Common adverse events were hypertension, elevated blood creatinine phosphokinase, and hot flushes.

Repeated 12-week courses of daily oral ulipristal acetate at either 5 or 10 mg doses was effective for control of bleeding and pain, reduced fibroid volume, and improved quality of life in patients with symptomatic fibroids.

Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole are also being used to treat fibroids, but data are limited. In one non-randomized trial of women undergoing laparoscopic myomectomy, the group receiving 3-month preoperative treatment with oral letrozole (2.5 mg/day) and norethindrone acetate (2.5 mg/day) had shorter operative times (122 min vs 134 min) and less intraoperative blood loss with no difference in major complications.

The antihyperlipidemic drug Simvastatin is under investigation for symptomatic uterine fibroids. Simvastatin was found to suppress the overactive signaling pathway Wnt/β-catenin which may have a beneficial effect on fibroids.
Four surgical options are available for women who elect surgery: UAE or uterine artery ligation, myomectomy, hysterectomy, and ablative techniques.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 85 studies with 17,789 patients found that at 5 years the reintervention risk was 7% (95% CI 4.8%–9.5%) for hysteroscopy which included hysteroscopic myomectomy and hysteroscopic radiofrequency ablation, 12% (95% CI 5.2 - 21.2%) for myomectomy, 14.4% (95% CI 9.8-19.6%) for UAE, and 53.9% (95% CI 47.2%–60.4%) for high intensity focused ultrasound.

Using a cohort study of 10,324 patients aged 18-50 years who had a first uterus-preserving procedure for fibroids, 7-year reintervention risk was 20.6% for myomectomy, 26.0% for UAE, 35.5% for endometrial ablation, and 37.0% for hysteroscopic myomectomy.
UAE can be selected by women who no longer desire childbearing but desire uterine preservation or are high risk for undergoing major surgery.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 7 RCTs (3 vs hysterectomy, 2 vs myomectomy, and 2 vs surgery) found patient satisfaction with UAE was similar to surgery with reduced length of the procedure, length of hospital stay, time to resumption of routine activities, and decreased likelihood of needing a blood transfusion. UAE was associated with a higher rate of minor short and long-term complications (e.g., vaginal discharge, fever, nausea, vomiting) higher re-admission rates, and an increased surgical reintervention rate (7% reintervention with hysterectomy and between 15% and 32% with UAE).

In an RCT of 254 patients with symptomatic fibroids in the UK, those who underwent myomectomy had a better fibroid-related quality of life at 2 years than those who underwent UAE (mean adjusted difference with complete case analysis of 8.0 points, 95% CI 1.8 to 14.1). However, the mean clinically-important score change reported in development of this instrument was 20 points.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies (9 observational and 4 RCTs) found that UAE had a higher reintervention rate (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.6-2.1; I2 = 39%) and hysterectomy rate (OR 4.0, 95% CI 3.4-4.7; I2 = 59%) compared to myomectomy at four-year follow-up. However, UAE was associated with a lower rate of early complications (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2-0.95; I2 = 25%) and lower readmission rate (OR 1.2; 95% CI 1.01-1.3; I2 = 0%) than myomectomy. Quality of life may be better for those undergoing myomectomy compared to UAE when evaluating RCTs.

Based on population data from England including 9443 and 6224 women underwent elective myomectomy or UAE, respectively, there is a 2.4-fold increased rate of hysterectomy and 44% increased risk of further uterine-preserving procedures as reintervention after UAE relative to myomectomy after a median of 7 years of follow-up.

With respect to cost-effectiveness, over a 2-year time horizon, UAE had a non-significant higher mean cost (difference £645; 95% CI -1381 to 2580), but with lower quality-adjusted life years (difference -0.09; 95% CI -0.11 to -0.04) compared to myomectomy. Similar results were observed over the 4-year time horizon.

strong.em: Perioperative interventions to reduce pain and nausea/vomiting

list.listitem: With respect to pain control following UAE, the addition of preprocedural oral oxycodone to morphine patient-controlled analgesia did not offer any analgesic advantage and caused more nausea and vomiting. Single dose dexamethasone may be useful for reducing pain and severe nausea and vomiting after UAE, based on a small RCT.

Use of a superior hypogastric nerve block may also reduce post-operative pain antiemetic use after UAE. However, in a retrospective study, superior hypogastric nerve block was less effective than epidural anesthesia for procedural pain and pain at 6 hours post-procedure.

In a meta-analysis of 54 studies, major complication rates from UAE were 2.9% (95% CI, 2.2%-3.8%); hysterectomy for resolution of a complication from UAE was 0.7% (95% CI, 0.5%-0.9%), readmission rate was 2.7% (95% CI, 1.9%-3.7%), and retreatment rate (UAE, myomectomy, or hysterectomy) was 5.3% (95% CI, 4.2%-6.4%) with follow-up ranging from 4 months to 5 years.
In 2 small RCTs of UAE, about 1 in 5 women required retreatment. This figure is similar to a large retrospective study of 454 women of whom 22% required additional surgical intervention.
Gynecologic fistulas may occur as a long-term complication in symptomatic women with a history of UAE.

Subsequent ovarian function at 1 year following UAE does not appear to be affected compared with ovarian sparing surgery, and a longer follow-up study found no differences in ovarian reserve between younger women (ages 26-29 years) treated for fibroids with UAE and matched control women.
In a case series, bleeding and patient satisfaction was improved for 50 Nigerian women who underwent trans-vaginal bilateral uterine artery ligation for symptomatic fibroids.
Myomectomy is an option for women who may wish to conceive in the future. This procedure may be completed abdominally, laparoscopically, or via hysteroscopy.

In one RCT, myomectomy and UAE were comparable for symptom relief and satisfaction. In another RCT of 163 women, quality of life ratings at 1 year were similar. In a 4-year follow-up of a multicenter RCT with 254 women randomized to UAE or myomectomy, there were no differences between groups in quality of life, bleeding scores, rates of amenorrhea, or heavy bleeding, with similar percentages of those who were still menstruating, reporting regular or fairly regular periods (75% and 77%, respectively).

Hysteroscopic resection in one or two separate procedures is recommended in the French guidelines for women desiring pregnancy who have submucosal fibroids less than 4 cm in length. Treatment of intramural fibroids does not appear to improve fertility.

Authors of a systematic review of 12 RCTs including 1783 patients comparing laparoscopic to abdominal myomectomy found that the laparoscopic approach significantly decreased blood loss, shortened the duration of postoperative ileus (OR - 10.91, 95% CI -18.72- - 3.11), and reduced the length of hospital stay (OR - 1.57, 95% CI -2.05- - 1.08), but at the risk of longer duration of operation (OR 16.10, 95% CI 6.52-25.67) and higher medical costs.

Similarly, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 studies including 6357 patients found robotic-assisted laparoscopic treatment superior to abdominal procedures with respect to lower blood loss/transfusions, complication rates, and hospital stay. Based on 2 studies in this report, robotic-assisted laparoscopic myomectomy was superior to laparoscopic myomectomy for lower cesarean section rate (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10–0.78) but operating time was on average 43 minutes longer; there were no other significant differences in outcomes between groups.
Predictors of surgical difficulties and complications following laparoscopic myomectomy were myoma size and location (Intramural myomas >8 cm and subserosal myomas >12 cm).

Predictors for need for transfusion were Black or African American and Asian races, Hispanic ethnicity, bleeding disorders, American Society of Anesthesiologists class III or IV physical status classification (severe systemic disease), and a preoperative hematocrit value ≤35.0% based on a retrospective cohort using the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database. These authors developed a risk stratification tool based on these findings.

strong.em: Perioperative interventions to reduce blood loss

list.listitem: In a Cochrane review evaluating intraoperative strategies to reduce bleeding with myomectomy, reduction in blood loss was shown for misoprostol, vasopressin, bupivacaine plus epinephrine, tranexamic acid, gelatin thrombin matrix, mesna, and pericervical tourniquet. There is no evidence that oxytocin and morcellation reduce blood loss and the clinical importance of bupivacaine plus epinephrine was small compared to the other treatments.
In one RCT, use of transcervical intralesional vasopressin injection during hysteroscopic myomectomy reduced intraoperative blood loss but did not reduce operative time.

Among patients undergoing myomectomy, prophylactic vasopressin significantly reduced intraoperative blood loss and associated morbidities compared with a passive control intervention based on a meta-analysis of 11 studies including 8 RCTs. ACOG recommends vasopressin infiltration of the myometrium to reduce bleeding.

In an RCT of 80 women undergoing myomectomy, women receiving oxytocin 30 IU in 500 ml normal saline vs normal saline alone had less intra-operative blood loss (189.5 ± 16.72 ml vs 692.25 ± 89.93 ml, respectively) and fewer blood transfusions (3 vs 10 women, respectively).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 studies of women undergoing abdominal myomectomy found perioperative tranexamic acid effective at reducing perioperative blood loss compared with no treatment or placebo, but there was no significant difference observed in blood transfusion requirement (RR 0.58; 95% CI 0.33-1.00).
UAE and temporary surgical ligature of the uterine arteries appear similar in reducing perioperative blood loss with myomectomy but UAE may be superior to pericervical tourniquet for this purpose.
Treatment of intramural fibroids does not appear to improve fertility.

Authors of a Cochrane review found no benefit with hysteroscopic myomectomy compared to fertility-oriented intercourse over 12 months for clinical pregnancy in a single RCT including women with otherwise unexplained subfertility and submucous fibroids. In a second Cochrane review (2 trials) there was no significant effect on live birth rate or other outcomes between open or laparoscopic myomectomy.

Investigators using a retrospective study of 311 patients with fibroids, of whom 165 eventually received myomectomy and 146 remained on expectant management, also found no difference in time to live birth after myomectomy compared with expectant management (adjusted hazard ratio 1.26, 95% CI 0.87-1.81).

Myomectomy may be superior to UAE among women planning future pregnancy. In a case series of 98 women who underwent UAE for symptomatic myomas, only 6 of 23 who expressed a wish to become pregnant had successful spontaneous conception.

Hysterectomy is optimal for women who no longer desire fertility and want definitive treatment. Hysterectomy avoids re-operation and is eventually required in about 25% of women attempting medical therapy. Of the three surgical approaches to hysterectomy (abdominal, vaginal, and laparoscopic), vaginal hysterectomy (VH) is better for all outcomes compared to abdominal hysterectomy (AH) and has shorter operating time and less bleeding compared to laparoscopic hysterectomy (LH); the latter may be preferred, however, if the vaginal approach is not possible. LH results in earlier return to normal activities, shorter hospital stay, and decreased risk of wound/abdominal wall infections and transfusion than AH, but is associated with more urinary tract injuries and longer operative times. When compared to LH, VH was comparable with respect to time to return to normal activities but associated with shorter operative time and shorter hospital stay. These authors caution that evidence in this review should be interpreted with caution as the low adverse event rates resulted in low power for these comparisons.

In an RCT of 108 women choosing hysterectomy for fibroids, the mean operating, paralytic ileus, and discharge times were shorter following VH than after laparoscopic VH or total laparoscopic hysterectomy. Intraoperative blood loss was greater during laparoscopic VH than during the other two procedures.
In another RCT for patients undergoing open AH or myomectomy, there was no clinically significant difference between epidural ropivacaine and subcutaneous ropivacaine on postoperative pain control.
Authors of a Cochrane review found no differences in surgical recovery or sexual, urinary or bowel function comparing subtotal hysterectomy with total abdominal hysterectomy for benign conditions.

Ablative techniques include myolysis (via laser or bipolar needles), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided focused ultrasound surgery, and installation of heated saline via hysteroscopy. There are limited data, primarily from case series, on these techniques.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 30 studies including only 3 RCTs found radiofrequency ablation successfully reduced uterine volume and improved quality of life scores for patients with symptomatic uterine fibroids. Post-procedure complications were infrequent but inconsistently reported. Most studies reported return to work and normal activities occurred within 2 weeks. Hysterectomy rates after ablation ranged from 1.0% to 24.1%. Insufficient data were available on fertility and there were few comparative studies available.
One trial comparing myolysis (bipolar) with heated saline found higher rates of amenorrhea (43% vs 8%) and patient satisfaction (90% vs 79%) at 12-month follow-up with myolysis.
In another RCT, radiofrequency volumetric thermal ablation resulted in a shorter hospital stay (median 7 vs 29.9 hours) and less intraoperative blood loss than laparoscopic myomectomy.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies comparing thermal ablative methods and myomectomy in 4205 patients with uterine fibroids found that ablative methods resulted in shorter hospital stays by -0.84 day in RCTs, and better symptom scores and quality of life; no differences were found in re-intervention or pregnancy rates.

In a combined RCT of 57 women and parallel cohort trial of 34 women refusing randomization, those undergoing MRI-guided focused ultrasound surgery had less post-procedural pain and shorter recovery time (4 days [2-7 days] vs 8 days [6-14 days]) compared with UAE. There were no significant differences in the incidence or severity of adverse events between treatment arms. Treatment effectiveness was not reported.

Factors associated with new/worsening pain or hysterectomy after endometrial ablation (occurring in 23% and 19% of 300 women, respectively) included, for pain: history of dysmenorrhea (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.74; 95% CI, 1.06-2.87), tubal sterilization (AOR 2.06; 95% CI, 1.14-3.70); white race was protective (AOR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.34-0.89). For subsequent hysterectomy, associated factors included a history of cesarean delivery (AOR 2.33; 95% CI, 1.05-5.16) and uterine abnormalities on imaging (AOR 3.96; 95% CI, 1.25-12.56).

At one-year follow-up of 51 women treated with ultrasound-guided suprapubic transvaginal radiofrequency ablation, symptom and quality-of-life scores had improved from 45 ± 14 and 65 ± 41, respectively, before treatment to 0 and 100 post treatment, no complications were reported and 41/45 were satisfied.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 studies with 28,661 patients, including 6 RCTs, of high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatment for uterine fibroids found higher re-intervention rates with ultrasound compared with UAE (RR 4.06, 95% CI 2.47-6.69, 6 studies) and UAE resulted in greater reduction in symptom severity score (mean difference 17.01, 95% CI 10.25-23.77) and improvement in health-related quality of life score (MD -18.32, 95% CI: -24.87 to -11.78).

A second meta-analysis including 10 studies including 4450 patients comparing HIFU with traditional surgery found a greater decrease in uterine fibroid severity score at 6- and 12-month with HIFU, faster return to work (MD – 11.61 days, 95% CI – 19.73 to – 3.50) and higher quality of life scores. There were similar results between the two groups for adverse events, symptom recurrence, re-intervention, and pregnancy.

Based on a meta-analysis of 18 studies from 7 databases, long-term outcomes of HIFU included a reintervention rate of 29% (95% CI 14-44%) at 60 months; rates were lower for US vs. MRI-guided procedures.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 25 articles found similar rates of live births following UAE, HIFU, and transcervical radiofrequency ablation of 70.8%, 70-73.5%, and 75%, respectively, although there were few cases of subsequent pregnancy for the transcervical approach.

HIFU was associated with higher pregnancy rates than UAE (RR 17.44, 95% CI 2.40-126.5) based on the meta-analysis cited above. Compared with traditional surgery based on 6 studies, there were no differences in re-intervention or pregnancy rates with HIFU.

The pregnancy rate after myomectomy in another meta-analysis was 0.43 (95% CI 0.36-0.49), which was higher than 0.18 (95% CI 0.10-0.26) after HIFU; both were significantly higher than pregnancy rates after UAE (0.08, 95% CI 0.06-0.10).

Myomectomy was also found to have significantly higher fertility and live birth rates (LBR) compared to HIFU in another meta-analysis. The pooled pregnancy rate for myomectomy was 56.9% (95% CI 45.6 to 67.9%) and pooled LBR was 44.1% (95% CI 34.9 to 53.4%) compared to 23.3% (95% CI 11.5 to 37.6%) and 17.3% (95% CI 7.8 to 29.3%), respectively, for HIFU.

A Cochrane review identified 41 randomized trials with 3982 women comparing a variety of medical therapies versus placebo or no treatment pre-operatively. GnRH analogues reduce uterine (175 ml) and fibroid (6 to 155 ml) volumes and increase hemoglobin, but increase the risk of adverse events (OR 2.8). They may reduce the duration of hysterectomy slightly (-10 minutes) and reduce blood transfusions and postoperative morbidity. Submucous myomas decrease fertility and may impair implantation rates in women undergoing assisted reproduction (OR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.48-0.8). Uterine fibroids do not appear to increase rates of spontaneous abortion.

Need for repeat intervention at 3 years following radiofrequency volumetric thermal ablation was 11% for 77% of the original 135 trial women; women also reported improved symptoms and quality of life over baseline.

In one cohort study of 1384 women undergoing treatment for uterine fibroids, although significant improvements were reported in health-related quality of life and symptom severity at 1-year posttreatment, there was a gradual decline in both health-related quality of life and symptom improvement by the third year after abdominal myomectomy, laparoscopic myomectomy or UAE.
There have been successful pregnancies reported following myomectomy, UAE, and ulipristal acetate treatment. B
The prevalence of uterine fibroids was 10.7% in one large study of pregnant women in the third trimester; prevalence was highest among African American women (18%).
Uterine myomas likely decrease in size during pregnancy.
Although large fibromas were associated with elective cesarean delivery in one study, there was no association with cesarean delivery during labor.

Authors of a meta-analysis of observational studies, however, found that uterine leiomyomas increased the risk of cesarean delivery (OR 2.60; 95% CI, 2.02-3.18) and malpresentation at term (OR 2.65; 95% CI, 1.60-3.70).
In a large Chinese population study, women with uterine fibroids had an increased risk of preterm birth (11% vs 7.8%) and SGA infants (19% vs 17.3%) compared to unaffected mothers.

Another large US cohort study of singleton pregnancies found that uterine fibroids identified on second trimester ultrasound (3.2% of women) were associated with small absolute increases in breech presentation (5.3% vs 3.1%; AOR 1.5; 95% CI, 1.3-1.9), placenta previa (1.4% vs 0.5%; AOR 2.2; 95% CI, 1.5-3.2), cesarean delivery (33.1% vs 24.2%; AOR 1.2; 95% CI, 1.1-1.4), placental abruption (1.4% vs 0.7%; AOR 2.1; 95% CI, 1.4-3.0), preterm birth less than 37 weeks (15.1% vs 10.5%; AOR 1.5; 95% CI, 1.3-1.8), and intrauterine fetal death in women with a growth restricted fetus (3.9% vs 1.5%; AOR 2.5; 95% CI, 1.2-5.0).

Risk of preterm birth at <37 weeks was confirmed to be higher among women with uterine fibroids, based on two meta-analyses - the first including 18 studies with 276,172 pregnancies which found a RR of 1.43, 95% CI 1.27-1.60, and the second including 11 studies with 256,650 singleton deliveries which found a higher rate of preterm births of 11.6% versus 9.0% (OR 1.66, 95%CI 1.29-2.14). In the former study, authors also found a higher risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes, fetal malpresentation, placental abruption, lower gestational age and birthweight at delivery and a higher cesarean delivery rate.

Pooled results from another meta-analysis including 24 studies demonstrated that fibroids elevated the risk of adverse outcomes including preterm birth, cesarean delivery, placenta previa, placental abruption, post-partum hemorrhage, intrauterine fetal death, breech presentation, and preeclampsia after adjusting for the potential confounding factors.
In a study of 2378 twin pregnancies, 2.3% had fibroid tumors and there was no association between fibroids and adverse outcomes including SGA and preterm delivery.

UAE and myomectomy are treatment options for uterine fibroids in women undergoing cesarean section; in a case control study, operative time was increased but recovery and complication rates were comparable and subsequent surgical intervention rate was lower (2.8% vs 41.7%).

Authors of a systematic review of 19 studies including 2,301 women undergoing myomectomy during cesarean delivery and 1,599 undergoing cesarean delivery alone found a mean of 13.87 minutes (95% CI, 4.78-22.95) longer operative time but no differences in major hemorrhage, postoperative blood transfusion or fever between groups. There was a clinically insignificant increase in hospital length of stay (mean difference 0.35 days, 95% CI, 0.25-0.46).

In the most recent meta-analysis including 23 non-randomized studies with 7504 patients, evidence was very uncertain about whether cesarean myomectomy affects risk of requiring blood transfusion compared to caesarean section alone (risk ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.79; I2 = 33%) or extends length of hospital stay (mean difference 0.30 days, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.51; I2= 93%). No studies reported here contained data on future fertility outcomes.

It is not clear if removal of uterine fibroids improves fertility. Based on one systematic review and meta-analysis, the clinical pregnancy rate for women undergoing myomectomy for intramural leiomyomas was no different than those with intramural leiomyomas in situ (OR 1.1, 95% CI, 0.8-1.6).
